qt: to the Commission Biljana Borzan (S&D) Subject:

Citizens complain about the increasingly limited availability of advanced digital and AI functionalities in certain Member States, particularly for smaller languages such as Croatian. Certain devices and services – including assistive technologies of crucial importance for blind and visually impaired people – offer a significantly wider range of features in some Member States than in others. However, this practice leads to unequal access to technologies and potential discrimination against citizens based on their language and place of residence, which contradicts the EU’s fundamental principles of equality and inclusion. Can the Commission clarify whether it considers such a practice to be compliant with EU law and whether it plans to issue additional guidance to ensure equal access to digital and AI solutions, particularly assistive technologies, for all EU citizens, regardless of language?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.11.2026) Accessibility is crucial to enable persons with disabilities to fully participate in all areas of life. Nevertheless, persons with disabilities continue to face barriers, including in access to services, information or digital communication tools. AI can be used as one type of assistive technology to support persons with disabilities, facilitating their autonomy and full integration into society. Under one of the flagship initiatives of the Communication ‘Enhancing the strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities up to 2030’1 the Commission will seek to promote better knowledge and strengthen the single market for assistive technologies and AI applications. The aim is to identify and remove bottlenecks that prevent persons with disabilities from benefiting from accessible and affordable technologies. The Commission will continue monitoring the implementation and application of the European Accessibility Act2, and providing support via the AccessibleEU resource centre3, as effective implementation of key legislation on accessibility remains a major focus up to 2030. As for the AI Act4, it aims, inter alia, to ensure a high level of protection of the fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union5, while harmonising rules governing AI systems and models on the EU market. However, it does not establish general requirements concerning the accessibility or availability of AI systems in different countries or for different linguistic groups.
